passage:
I'm Hemant, and I wanted to tell you properly, Ramesh sir, because you asked why I stopped coming to the running club.
When we moved here in June I didn't know anyone. Then some seniors invited me to the Circle. It started with morning runs, and it was brilliant. They knew my name on the first day. Wristbands, a chant before every run, "brother" this, "brother" that. For the first time here I felt like I belonged.
Then it changed. Five a.m. meetings, then weekends. Last week the leader told me my old friends from class "hold me back". And he said, "Don't tell your parents about the Circle yet. They won't get it."
That made my stomach go cold.
You listened to all of it, sir, and you didn't laugh. You said wanting friends was completely normal, and hiding a group from my family was the warning sign. Then you called my mum while I was still sitting here.

qa.q: What did the leader say about Hemant's old friends from class?
qa.a: The leader said Hemant's old friends from class "hold me back".

qa.q: Why did the Circle feel so good to Hemant at first?
qa.a: Hemant had moved in June and knew nobody, so being known by name, the chant and being called "brother" gave him a strong feeling of belonging.

qa.q: What was the turning point that made Hemant ask for help?
qa.a: Being told not to tell his parents about the Circle made his stomach go cold, and he recognised the secrecy as a warning and went to Ramesh sir.

qa.q: How does Ramesh sir respond to what Hemant tells him?
qa.a: Ramesh sir listens without laughing, tells Hemant that wanting friends is normal and that hiding a group is the warning sign, and calls Hemant's mum that same day.

grounding: A lonely teenager is drawn into an intense group offering quick friendship and rituals, recognises the danger when told to hide it and cut off others, and tells Ramesh sir.

passage:
Nilesh and I have been in the same hostel wing since Class 8, so I noticed when he changed.
This term he started leaving the common room early for "calls with the group". He wore the same grey thread on his wrist every day. He started saying "the awakened" and "sleepers", and when I asked who the sleepers were, he said, "People like you, Tenzin. No offence."
He laughed differently, sort of far away. He stopped coming to Saturday football. I think he was lonely after his best mate left in April, but I don't know that for sure.
Then last Thursday I saw a message on his screen: "Delete this chat. Your warden must not know."
I went to Mrs D'Souza, our house parent, that evening. She listened, thanked me and said telling was right. Before dinner she sat with Nilesh in her office for a long time, and she called his parents that night.

qa.q: What did the message on Nilesh's screen say?
qa.a: It said, "Delete this chat. Your warden must not know."

qa.q: What does Tenzin think might be behind Nilesh's change, and how sure is Tenzin?
qa.a: Tenzin thinks Nilesh may have been lonely after his best mate left in April, but openly says it is only a guess.

qa.q: Which moment made Tenzin act, and was it the right step?
qa.a: The message telling Nilesh to hide the chat from his warden; taking it to the house parent that same evening was right because secrecy is the warning sign.

qa.q: How does Mrs D'Souza respond once Tenzin tells her?
qa.a: Mrs D'Souza listens, thanks Tenzin, sits with Nilesh in her office before dinner and calls his parents that night.

grounding: Tenzin notices a hostel-mate drawn into a secretive group with rituals and new words, and reports it once the group demands secrecy; the house parent acts the same day.
